title: Chapter 98: Hensheng: To Hate Life 1
content:
Chapter 98

Hensheng: To Hate Life 1

Wei Wuxian took Wen Ning and headed straight for the Guanyin Temple downtown. He and Lan Wangji had scoped the place out earlier that afternoon, planning to circle back under the cover of darkness to crack the suppression array, uncover whatever was locked beneath it, and see if it could give them some leverage against Jin Guangyao. Who knew he’d sleep clean through till eight in the evening—or that things would spiral into that catastrophic mess the moment he woke up? With their original timetable completely derailed and a toxic cloud of restless misery gnawing at his ribs, crashing Jin Guangyao’s secret stash felt like the perfect way to vent some steam.

The dead of night had hollowed out the streets. Shutters were latched tight, lanterns were out, and the heavy double doors of the Guanyin Temple were barred shut. Looking past the towering perimeter wall, the courtyard appeared steeped in pitch-black silence. But the second Wei Wuxian scaled the bricks, freezing just below the roofline, his gut fired an instant alarm.

Something’s wrong.

Beside him, Wen Ning went rigid as stone, his voice dropping to a rasp: "A barrier."

Wei Wuxian flashed a quick hand signal. They slipped down to the dirt without a whisper of sound, gave the front entrance a wide berth, and crept toward an unmonitored blind spot around the temple's rear. Prowling up the masonry with feather-light precision, they tucked themselves behind a carved roof-beast, cautiously peering down into the grounds below.

The scene knocked the air right out of both of them.

Bathed in blinding torchlight, the inner courtyard was crawling with people. Half were shaved-headed monks; the other half wore the shimmering, gold-embroidered Sparks-Amidst-Snow robes of the Lanling Jin Sect. Both factions stood shoulder to shoulder, bows drawn and steel unsheathed, on hair-trigger guard like a garrison bracing for a siege, exchanging only terse, muttered murmurs. The temple was sealed behind a specialized illusion ward: from the street outside, the compound looked like a quiet, pitch-black tomb, completely swallowing the blazing light and muffled chatter within.

Yet what made Wei Wuxian’s jaw drop wasn't the ward, nor the armed retinue of fake monks and cult-disciples.

It was the white-robed figure standing dead-center in the courtyard.

Lan Xichen.

No ropes, no talismans, no visible bindings. Even his spiritual sword, Shuoyue, and his white jade xiao, Liebing, hung casually at his hip. He stood amidst the crowd with uncanny, placid poise, while the monks and cultivators treated him with nervous deference, bowing and scraping to his every word.

Wei Wuxian took in the field, then leaned close to Wen Ning’s ear. "Sprint back to the inn. Drag Hanguang-jun here. Now."

Wen Ning nodded once and melted into the gloom.

Wei Wuxian scanned the courtyard. No sign of Jin Guangyao yet, leaving it a coin toss whether the man had already arrived or if the Yin Tiger Tally was nestled in his sleeve. After a beat of calculation, he brought a thumb to his teeth, bit down to draw blood, and angled the crimson bead toward the mouth of the spirit-trapping pouch at his hip. He needed to coax a few low-level wraiths out to quietly herd some heavy malice to his position.

Before the blood could smear the pouch, a vicious chorus of barking shattered the silence from the far end of the street.

Wei Wuxian’s soul nearly shot out of his mouth.

A wave of gut-wrenching terror hit him so hard he had to white-knuckle the stone eaves just to stop himself from launching into orbit. Shaking like a leaf, clinging for dear life to the roof-beast, he listened to the savage barking close the distance, frantically crying out in his head: Save me, Lan Zhan! Lan Zhan, save me!

Calling on that name gave his frayed nerves just enough spine to pull his breath together. He desperately prayed it was just some stray mongrel that would keep trotting down the road, but the heavens had zero interest in cutting him a break. Slicing through the racket came the bright, sharp snap of a young man’s voice, spitting mad:

"Fairy, shut the hell up! It’s the middle of the night—are you trying to wake up the entire block?!"

Jin Ling!

Lan Xichen’s brow pinched. Down below, the Lanling Jin cultivators instantly clocked their young master's voice; eyes locked across the ranks as archers drew their bows to their ears. Jin Ling’s footsteps were fast, skidding to a halt outside the main gates within seconds.

"Hush! Shut up! Bark again and I'm turning you into stew! ...Where the hell are you even dragging me?"

Perched on the wall, Wei Wuxian’s heart was doing frantic backflips. You little disaster magnet, get the hell out of here!

Naturally, Jin Ling didn't budge. Outside, Fairy whined and scratched at the masonry, tearing at the dirt like a dog possessed. Jin Ling sounded genuinely baffled: "Here? Seriously?"

A brief pause. Then, the sound of heavy fists hammering on the wood: "Anyone in there?!"

Inside the walls, every cultivator held their breath, nocked arrows aimed dead at the gates, waiting for the order to loose.

Lan Xichen called out softly, "Do not harm him!"

His voice was smothered by the barrier, unable to reach the street, and the men didn't lower their bows by a millimeter. On the other side of the timber, Jin Ling seemed to smell the rat. Even if the night watch was dead asleep, pounding on the door hard enough to rattle the hinges should have woken the dead; a temple staying this dead silent was outright wrong. The knocking died away.

Wei Wuxian had barely begun to unclench when a fresh burst of barking exploded outside, followed by Jin Ling’s exasperated shout: "Hey! Why are you running back the other way?!"

Wei Wuxian’s eyes lit up with pure, tearful gratitude: Good dog! Beautiful dog!

"Fairy! Get back here! Dammit!"

Keep running, kid! Wei Wuxian pleaded silently. Follow your damn dog and bolt! I'm begging you!

Instead, the faint, rustling scrape of loose masonry broke the quiet. Wei Wuxian frowned, trying to place the sound—and cold sweat broke out across his spine.

Shit. The brat is scaling the wall.

On the far ridge, Jin Ling cleared the parapet, his eyes going wide at the sea of drawn arrows pointed squarely at his chest. Down in the courtyard, a monk who either didn't recognize the young heir or was dead set on leaving no loose ends simply loosed his fingers.

The arrow tore through the night with a murderous shriek.

By the pitch of the wind alone, Wei Wuxian knew the archer was lethal. If that shaft hit, it would punch clean through Jin Ling’s chest and snap his spine. He had only one thing on hand that could intercept the shot. Throwing himself onto the crest of the wall, he whipped his arm forward, bellowing: "Jin Ling, run!"

The bamboo flute he’d carried since waking up in Mo Xuanyu’s body cut through the air, colliding with the iron tip. The shaft was knocked wildly off course, while the green bamboo shattered into splinters. Jin Ling’s silhouette dropped back down the street side of the wall—he’d bolted.

But Wei Wuxian was blown wide open. A black rain of over a hundred fletched arrows blackened the sky, turning the carved stone beast he’d been hiding behind into a pincushion within a breath.

Wei Wuxian scrambled, his heart pounding. Every single one of these bastards is a master marksman with real spiritual juice. Whether Jin Ling could actually shake them was suddenly looking dicey.

Vaulting off the wall, Wei Wuxian brought his fingers to his lips to loose a whistle—only for an amused, silky voice to glide up from right behind his shoulder:

"I’d strongly advise Master Wei against that. Flutes are easy to replace; your fingers and your tongue, considerably less so."

Wei Wuxian dropped his hand without a second's hesitation, offering an agreeable nod. "Fair point. Can't argue with that."

The voice murmured pleasantly, "Shall we?"

Wei Wuxian gave a polite nod. "After you, Sect Leader Jin."

Jin Guangyao’s smile was all warmth. "You're too kind."

The two took an absurdly leisurely stroll around the perimeter, sauntering through the front gates as though dropping by for afternoon tea. Wei Wuxian looked around, thoroughly deadpan.

The temple doors hung wide open. Jin Ling hadn't escaped after all—he was cornered, held at the point of several gleaming swords. Catching sight of the arrivals, the boy hesitated, finally choking out:

"...Youngest Uncle."

Jin Guangyao offered a charming, paternal smile. "Good evening, A-Ling."
